disease_info: Binge-Eating Disorder is characterized by recurrent episodes of consuming unusually large amounts of food in a discrete period while experiencing a sense of loss of control, followed by marked distress such as shame, guilt, or disgust. Unlike Bulimia Nervosa, it is not regularly accompanied by inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as purging, fasting, or excessive exercise. It is commonly associated with obesity or weight fluctuations, body image concerns, and mood or anxiety symptoms, and often follows a chronic, fluctuating course that can be exacerbated by stress, dieting, and emotional triggers. Onset can occur in adolescence or adulthood and is frequently linked to attempts at rigid dietary restraint, emotional coping through food, or longstanding patterns of using eating to manage distress.

narrative.personality: Janet is a quietly analytical, introverted woman who values order, self-discipline, and solitary hobbies like gardening, reading, and knitting, and takes pride in running her stores efficiently and frugally.
narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Janet’s retail chain went through a major restructuring that left her supervising more locations with fewer supports, longer hours, and constant pressure to hit aggressive performance metrics. Already inclined toward self-criticism, she responded by tightening her routines, skipping breaks, and adopting increasingly rigid eating rules during the day so she could “stay sharp” and avoid any sign of weakness at work. Over the next several months, the combination of chronic fatigue, solitary late evenings at home after closing shifts, and her perfectionistic tendency to see small slips as failures led her into a pattern of secretive, increasingly chaotic eating when she finally stopped working at night, which she rationalized at first as a deserved reward. After more than a year of this cycle, she found that the way she was eating at home starkly contradicted her image of herself as controlled and efficient, and the mounting self-disgust and embarrassment about these episodes finally pushed her to seek psychiatric help at her primary care physician’s urging.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel absolutely disgusted with myself and horribly guilty after these eating episodes.”

narrative.personality: Richard is a disciplined, detail-oriented retiree who prefers structured routines, quiet intellectual pursuits, and carefully planned community projects over spontaneity or emotional display.
narrative.stressor: Following his formal retirement and the winding down of his small business responsibilities, Richard’s days became far less structured, leaving him with long stretches of unplanned time despite his volunteering at the historical society. He initially enjoyed the freedom to read, cook, and attend cultural events, but he also felt a subtle loss of identity and purpose that he was reluctant to admit, even to his wife. Over the next year, he began to rely more on solitary evening meals and snacks in front of his reading or television as a way to fill time and soothe a vague restlessness, gradually abandoning the slower, ritualized meals he once prided himself on preparing. When he noticed that he was starting to eat very quickly during these periods, barely registering the food and feeling oddly unsettled afterward, he became concerned that this new pattern was out of character and mentioned it to his primary care doctor, who referred him for psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I’ve been eating much faster than I ever used to, almost like I’m rushing through my meals without thinking.”

narrative.personality: Sheila is a warm, practical, community-minded woman who blends Southern hospitality with a love of gardening, church life, and mentoring younger people, while quietly taking on more responsibilities than she admits.
narrative.stressor: About fourteen months ago, Sheila’s adult daughter and two young grandchildren moved back into her home after a difficult separation, suddenly increasing Sheila’s caregiving load and emotional responsibilities. Between coordinating the community garden, organizing church events, and now managing school runs, homework, and her daughter’s emotional turmoil, Sheila began to feel constantly "on call" and had little time or privacy to process her own feelings. Gradually, late evenings in the kitchen became one of the few moments when she was alone and not expected to be strong, and she started using food as a way to decompress, finding that once she started she had trouble stopping, especially after particularly tense family interactions. As this pattern intensified over the year and she realized she was repeatedly eating in ways that felt out of her control and left her feeling spiritually and personally out of alignment with the self-discipline she tried to model, she confided in a church friend, who encouraged her to seek professional help.
narrative.chief_complaint: “When I get started eating in the evenings, it feels like I just can’t stop or control how much I’m eating.”
